operations.old: [L4] Complex conjugation satisfies the usual algebraic laws ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).
operations.new:
[L4] Complex conjugation satisfies the usual algebraic laws ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[L5] Gram–Schmidt turns a finite real or complex independent list into an orthonormal list with the same span, including the empty list ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]).

operations.description: Replace defective proof with complete conjugation-compatible eigenspace construction; Statement unchanged
operations.old:
1.1 Choose an orthonormal basis of $V$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be the matrix of $T$. By [L1], $AA^{\mathsf T}=A^{\mathsf T}A$. Because $A$ has real entries, its conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$ is still $A^{\mathsf T}$, so $A$ is a normal complex matrix on $\mathbb C^n$ with the standard Hermitian inner product from [L3]. Therefore [L2] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\mathbb C^n$ for $A$. [L1, L2, L3]

1.2 If $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ is an eigenvalue and $v=u+iw$ is a corresponding complex eigenvector, then $Au+iAw=Av=\lambda v=\lambda u+i\lambda w$, so $Au=\lambda u$ and $Aw=\lambda w$; hence one of $u,w$ is a nonzero real eigenvector, and repeating inside each real eigenspace yields orthonormal real eigenvectors for the real eigenvalues. [L4, algebra]

2.1 If $\lambda=a+ib$ with $b\ne0$ and $v=u+iw$ is a unit eigenvector, then $A\overline v=\overline\lambda\,\overline v$ because $A$ is real; since $\lambda\ne\overline\lambda$, the vectors $v$ and $\overline v$ are orthogonal in the orthonormal eigenbasis from step 1.1, so writing out $\langle v,\overline v\rangle=0$ and using [L4] gives $\|u\|^2-\|w\|^2+2i\langle u,w\rangle=0$, hence $\|u\|=\|w\|$ and $\langle u,w\rangle=0$. Also $A(u+iw)=(a+ib)(u+iw)=(au-bw)+i(bu+aw)$, so $Au=au-bw$ and $Aw=bu+aw$; after normalising $e_1=u/\|u\|$ and $e_2=w/\|w\|$, the matrix of $A$ on $\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$. [L4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The orthonormal complex eigenbasis from step 1.1 splits into real eigenvectors and conjugate pairs. Step 1.2 replaces each real eigenvector by a real one, and step 2.1 replaces each conjugate pair by an orthonormal real pair spanning the same real invariant plane. Collecting these mutually orthogonal pieces yields an orthonormal real basis with the stated block-diagonal matrix. [step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎
operations.new:
1.1 Apply [L5] to a basis of $V$ to choose an orthonormal basis, and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be the matrix of $T$. By [L1], $AA^{\mathsf T}=A^{\mathsf T}A$. Since $A$ has real entries, its conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$ is $A^{\mathsf T}$, so $A$ is normal on $\mathbb C^n$ with the standard Hermitian inner product from [L3]. Thus [L2] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$, say $Az_j=\mu_jz_j$. If $n=0$, all subsequent lists are empty and give the asserted empty block decomposition. [L1, L2, L3, L5, choose]

1.2 For each eigenvalue $\lambda$, write $E_\lambda=\ker_{\mathbb C}(A-\lambda I)$. Expanding $x=\sum_j c_jz_j$ gives $(A-\lambda I)x=\sum_j(\mu_j-\lambda)c_jz_j$, so $E_\lambda$ is exactly the span of the $z_j$ with $\mu_j=\lambda$. Consequently these vectors form an orthonormal basis of the entire eigenspace, the distinct eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal, and their sum is $\mathbb C^n$. Also $A\overline x=\overline{Ax}$ by reality of $A$, so conjugation maps $E_\lambda$ onto $E_{\overline\lambda}$, with itself as inverse. [step 1.1, L4, algebra]

1.3 For real $\lambda$, put $R_\lambda=\ker_{\mathbb R}(A-\lambda I)$. If $x=u+iw\in E_\lambda$ with $u,w\in\mathbb R^n$, comparison of real and imaginary parts gives $u,w\in R_\lambda$; conversely every such $u+iw$ lies in $E_\lambda$. Choose a real basis of the finite-dimensional subspace $R_\lambda$ and apply [L5] to obtain a real orthonormal basis. It also spans $E_\lambda$ over $\mathbb C$ by the decomposition just proved, and is complex-linearly independent: the real and imaginary parts of a complex linear relation are real relations among that real basis. Thus it is a full orthonormal complex basis of $E_\lambda$, consisting of real eigenvectors. [step 1.2, L4, L5, choose, algebra]

2.1 For each conjugate pair of nonreal eigenvalues, select the representative $\lambda=a+ib$ with $b>0$. Choose an orthonormal basis $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ of $E_\lambda$ from step 1.2 and use $\overline v_1,\ldots,\overline v_m$ for $E_{\overline\lambda}$. Conjugation is bijective between these eigenspaces and satisfies $\langle\overline v_j,\overline v_k\rangle=\overline{\langle v_j,v_k\rangle}=\delta_{jk}$, so this is a full orthonormal basis there. Step 1.2 also gives $\langle v_j,\overline v_k\rangle=0$ for every $j,k$. [step 1.2, L3, L4, choose, algebra]

2.2 Write $v_j=u_j+iw_j$ with real $u_j,w_j$. Using the coordinate pairing, the identities $\langle v_j,v_k\rangle=\delta_{jk}$ and $\langle v_j,\overline v_k\rangle=0$ give respectively $u_j\cdot u_k+w_j\cdot w_k=\delta_{jk}$, $w_j\cdot u_k-u_j\cdot w_k=0$, $u_j\cdot u_k-w_j\cdot w_k=0$, and $w_j\cdot u_k+u_j\cdot w_k=0$. Hence $u_j\cdot u_k=w_j\cdot w_k=\delta_{jk}/2$ and $u_j\cdot w_k=w_j\cdot u_k=0$. Therefore $e_j=\sqrt2u_j$ and $f_j=\sqrt2w_j$ form an orthonormal real list. Comparing parts in $A(u_j+iw_j)=(a+ib)(u_j+iw_j)$ gives $Ae_j=ae_j-bf_j$ and $Af_j=be_j+af_j$. Thus each ordered pair $(e_j,f_j)$ spans an invariant plane with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$. Moreover $u_j=(v_j+\overline v_j)/2$ and $w_j=(v_j-\overline v_j)/(2i)$, so these real vectors have complex span exactly $E_\lambda\oplus E_{\overline\lambda}$. [step 2.1, L3, L4, algebra, construct]

3.1 Collect the real bases from step 1.3 and the real pairs from step 2.2 for every selected nonreal representative. Vectors from different groups are orthogonal: each group lies in the complex span of its own eigenspace or conjugate eigenspace pair, and these disjoint groups of eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal by step 1.2; for real vectors the Hermitian pairing is the real dot product. Within each group orthonormality was proved in steps 1.3 and 2.2. Their complex span is all of $\mathbb C^n$ by step 1.2. Since the collected vectors are real, taking real parts of a complex expansion of any $x\in\mathbb R^n$ shows that they span $\mathbb R^n$ over $\mathbb R$. They therefore give a real orthonormal basis, including the empty basis when $n=0$. Each basis vector from step 1.3 contributes $[\lambda]$, and each pair from step 2.2 contributes the displayed block with $b>0$, hence $b\ne0$. Transporting this basis through the coordinates of step 1.1 gives the required orthonormal basis of $V$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎
